title: Progressively Sampled Equality-Constrained Optimization
contribution: Extends progressive (adaptive) sample-size methods to equality-constrained SAA problems in which both objective and constraints are sampled, proving a better worst-case second-order sample-complexity bound than a one-shot full-sample solve when the initial sample is large enough, and showing data-access savings on a 2-D problem and a PINN.
problem_entry: Lifts Mokhtari-Ozdaglar-Jadbabaie's unconstrained progressive sampling to sampled constraints, naming what breaks: constrained second-order complexity, a constrained termination test (least-squares multipliers), and acute-perturbation geometry of sampled Jacobians (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: Solve nested sampled problems with geometrically growing sample sets, warm-starting each at the previous output and stopping at (eps_k, zeta_k)-stationarity; any solver with a cold-start O(max{eps^-2, zeta^-3}) bound and a warm-start log bound gives the total sample bound (Algorithm 1 p. 6; Theorem 3.1 pp. 17-18).
assumptions: Uniform smallest-singular-value bound for sampled Jacobians with |S| >= p1, solver convergence to second-order points, (alpha, beta)-strongly Morse full problem, bounded derivatives, deterministic finite-population variance bounds; high-probability versions admitted as possible but not used; infeasible stationary points excluded (pp. 6-8).
proof_devices: finite-population sampling bound via Cauchy-Schwarz giving errors proportional to xi_S = sqrt(N(N-|S|))/|S| (Lemma 3.2, p. 9)
acute perturbation of sampled vs full Jacobians once |S| exceeds a threshold proportional to N, via singular-value perturbation (Lemma 3.3, p. 10)
Stewart (1977) pseudo-inverse perturbation theory to bound least-squares multiplier differences, correcting a typo in Stewart's Theorem 5.2 (Lemma 3.4, pp. 11-13)
inheritance of strong Morse-ness by sampled problems via null-space/range decomposition (Lemmas 3.5-3.6, pp. 13-17)

tolerances eps_k = tau1 xi_{S_k} put each warm start inside the next problem's strongly Morse region; local strong convexity of Fletcher's augmented Lagrangian gives log2(5 omega eps_k/eps_{k+1}) gradient-descent iterations (Lemmas A.1, A.4, pp. 24-26, 33-34)
geometric sum of |S_k| log terms for the total bound (Theorem A.1, pp. 37-38)
experiments: Matlab; measure = individual constraint-gradient/data accesses; 2-D sin/cos-perturbed problem (N = 2048) with strong-Morse constants checked by contour plots, p1 = 64 vs one-shot, two subproblem solvers (Fletcher-AL second-order and first-order SQP); PINN for a damped oscillator with a 10x10 grid of initial sample sizes, best (16,32) about 35% of one-shot data accesses; in-house geometric-increase rival (27 settings) all worse; repeats per cell not reported (pp. 19-23).
positioning: Constrained counterpart of Mokhtari et al.; builds on recent second-order complexity work for equality constraints (Goyens-Eftekhari-Boumal; Dimou-O'Neill) and Stewart's perturbation theory; adaptive-sampling literature engaged only through an in-house imitation (pp. 2-3, 9-13, 23).
writing: 'We propose, analyze, and test' opening and closing; each assumption followed by a mildness argument; 'formal remarks' flagged as important; Remark 3.3 pre-empts the |S| proportional to N objection; theorem text admits p1 is unknown in practice; one-paragraph conclusion (pp. 2, 7, 10, 17, 23).
limits_future: Needed sample size is a fixed fraction of N; valid p1 unknown in practice; deterministic assumptions; infeasible stationary points ruled out; appendix covers constraint sampling only; no future-work section (pp. 6-11, 17, 23-24).

method_links.note: Subproblem tolerances are derived from what the outer progressive-sampling scheme needs (warm start must land in the next strongly Morse region), but the outer object is a sample-size schedule, not a merit function.

One-shot baseline is the same algorithm with p1 = N and the same solver, and the adaptive-sampling rival is built in-house with one component changed; but the rival is run only at the progressive method's best start chosen from the evaluation grid, and repeats are not reported.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Outer sample bound proved against a stated cold-start/warm-start complexity contract for any subproblem solver, then instantiated with one solver in a corollary.

Tie the inner stopping tolerance to the sampling-error scale with a +1 so the final tolerance does not vanish: eps_k = 1e-6 sqrt(N(N-|S_k|)/|S_k|^2 + 1) (eq. (43), p. 20).

title: Active-Set Identification in Noisy and Stochastic Optimization
contribution: Proves that two active-set identification procedures (Oberlin-Wright's LP-LPEC multiplier route and a new l1-penalty QP primal-step route) still identify the optimal active set from a nearby point when all function and derivative values carry small bounded deterministic or stochastic errors, with corollaries inside stochastic algorithms and 2-D and constrained-NN illustrations.
problem_entry: Classical identification guarantees assume exact values plus a CQ; little extends them to errors, and the one exception (Na-Anitescu-Kolar) is algorithm-specific with exact constraints (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: Keep the identification subproblems and thresholds, feed them noisy data, and bound the effect; replace Oberlin-Wright's LP-with-trust-region by an always-feasible l1-penalty QP with proximal term because noisy-setting algorithms already solve such QPs (pp. 5-8, 14-15).
assumptions: Uniform deterministic error bounds on f, e, c and gradients (covers deterministic and stochastic noise); LP-LPEC route: MFCQ + second-order condition with x-dependent noise tolerance (noise reduction near x*); QP route: LICQ + strict complementarity at a strict local minimizer with a uniform tolerance; stochastic corollaries assume a.s. convergence of iterates and per-iteration probability p of small noise (pp. 10, 14, 17-19).
proof_devices: exact QP route: contradiction over finitely many index sets, closedness of the finitely generated cone (Rockafellar Thm 19.1), dual QP objective lower vs upper bound with theta <= ||x - x*||^-zeta (Theorem 3.3, pp. 8-10)
sign-pattern bookkeeping (PP, PN, NP, NN) and a mean-value bound on the square root to bound noisy vs exact rho-bar (Lemma 4.2, pp. 11-14)
noisy QP solution = solution of the KKT linear system on A(x*); linear-system perturbation bound keeps d near 0 and multipliers positive (Lemma 2.1, Lemma 4.4, pp. 5, 16-17)
Han-Mangasarian exact-penalty theory makes slacks zero for nu large (Theorem 4.2, p. 17)
two-line stochastic corollaries: a.s. convergence puts X_k in the identification ball (Theorems 4.3-4.4, pp. 18-19)
experiments: Two strongly convex 2-D problems (one/two active constraints), grid heatmaps of exact-identification fraction under uniform noise 0, 1e-2, 1e-1 with 8 instances per point; constrained NN on UCI heart disease (91 variables, 10 group monotonicity constraints, test = top-20% cholesterol) solved by quadratic-penalty L-BFGS, test accuracy 78.5% -> 83.9%, identification tracked along iterates with exact data and with 10 minibatch(32) resamplings; host solver is deterministic (pp. 19-24).
positioning: 'Following primarily' Oberlin-Wright; credits the deterministic-noise literature (Nocedal group, Waechter, own work) and stochastic-constrained literature (much his own); the closest competitor is described by its scope (pp. 3, 8, 25-27).
writing: Contribution as 'showing that such guarantees can be extended'; organization separates one new exact-setting result from the main noisy contributions; intuitive paragraph on what theta and nu thresholds do; explicit hedges on numerical comparisons; NN constraints flagged as for demonstration only (pp. 3-4, 10, 20, 24).
limits_future: Purely local results needing small noise (x-dependent for LP-LPEC); comparisons parameter-dependent. Future: noisy active-set algorithms that estimate the set then compute directions on it; extending equality-only multiplier guarantees to inequalities (pp. 14, 18, 20, 25).

method_links.note: The identification test is built on the QP the outer noisy-setting algorithm already solves for its search direction; the inner subproblem serves a second purpose rather than having its accuracy set by the globalization.
Attributes LP-LPEC's early identification success to all iterates being infeasible ('lucky'), and QP's better noisy count to over-prediction, rather than crediting the methods.
Reports where each procedure wins and narrows the claim to parameter-dependent, problem-dependent comparisons.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Exact-data identification theorem carried to noisy data by the classical perturbation bound for nonsingular linear systems (S092 does the same with pseudo-inverse perturbation).

transferable: Define one noise model as uniform error bounds on every function and derivative value so a single proof covers deterministic and stochastic noise (eq. (23), p. 10).
Write the identification test as the solution of a nonsingular linear system on the optimal active set and apply the standard Kv = b perturbation bound (Lemma 4.4, pp. 16-17).
Contrast two procedures by the shape of their noise requirement (point-dependent with noise reduction vs uniform in a neighbourhood) (pp. 14, 17-18).
Record at every iterate of an ordinary solver run how many elements of the final active set a procedure gets right, with exact data and with several minibatch resamplings (pp. 23-24).
Impose one max-constraint per data group rather than per point to keep a constrained-learning test problem tractable, and report the effect on test accuracy (pp. 20, 23).

quotes.text: this demonstrates a situation in which the LP-LPEC approach is lucky always to identify violated constraints as being active at the optimal solution.
Naturally, the behavior of the methods can vary with these parameter choices, so these comparisons do not necessarily hold in general.

title: A single-loop stochastic feasible interior-point algorithm for nonlinear inequality-constrained optimization
contribution: Proposes SLIP, a single-loop feasible interior-point framework using stochastic objective gradients and no objective values for problems with linear equalities and nonlinear inequalities, proves liminf stationarity (deterministic) and almost-sure liminf stationarity (stochastic) with KKT limits under LICQ, and demonstrates it on 327 CUTEst problems, an SOCP and a norm-constrained NN.
problem_entry: IPMs dominate deterministic nonconvex practice but have barely been extended to stochastic gradients; three obstacles named: nested loops need an uncomputable inner stationarity test, barrier gradients are not Lipschitz or bounded, globalization needs function values (p. 2).
key_idea: Replace the nested loop by prescribed coupled decay of barrier and neighbourhood parameters (mu_k/theta_{k-1} constant), keep iterates in shrinking neighbourhoods {c <= -theta}, take one projected (stochastic) barrier-gradient step whose direction moves away from nearly active constraints, with a step factor gamma_k keeping the segment feasible (pp. 6-9, 12).
assumptions: f, c C1, strictly feasible point exists (no nonlinear equalities), A full row rank; Lipschitz/bounded constants on iterate segments; nonstandard Assumption 2 that a direction satisfying (6) always exists (nondegeneracy + mu1/theta0 large), examined via a holding and a failing example; unbiased gradients with almost-surely bounded projected error; uniformly bounded H_k (pp. 3, 5, 8-9, 18, 25-29).
proof_devices: shifted barrier with log(-c_i/kappa_ci): same gradient, bounded below by f_inf, increasing in mu, so barrier decreases never hurt (pp. 9-10)
local Lipschitz constant of the barrier gradient on the neighbourhood N(theta) (Lemma 2, p. 10)
gamma_k as positive root of the quadratic upper model of c_i along the step, with a uniform lower bound from a nearly-active / not-nearly-active case split (Lemmas 3-4, pp. 12-14)
sufficient decrease and non-summability of gamma_k alpha_k under polynomial schedules with t_mu = t_theta; multipliers z_k = -mu_k/c(x_k) give KKT limits under LICQ (Lemma 5, Theorem 1, pp. 15-17)

run-independent band [gamma_min, gamma_max] with a k^t buffer and a sign split of the noise inner product via the Law of Total Expectation to handle correlation between step factor and noise (Parameter Rule 2, Lemma 9, pp. 19-23)
exponent conditions t + t_alpha in [-1,0), 2t + t_alpha < -1, t + 2t_alpha < -1 for summable noise, then Fatou's lemma for a.s. liminf (Lemma 11, Theorem 2, pp. 19, 23-25)
experiments: No level-playing-field competitor, so no external baseline. Deterministic Python SLIP on CUTEst: 1315 -> 396 (filters on problem type/size) -> 327 after a separate Phase I failed on 59 and 10 evaluation errors; t = 0.7, Lipschitz constants estimated from random points, mu1 doubled (cap 1e4) when (6) fails, 2e4 iterations; f decreased on all runs; histogram of a relative stationarity measure. Stochastic: random SOCP with Gaussian gradient noise and mushrooms NN with minibatch 256, 10 seeds each, all printed against the deterministic twin (pp. 30-34).
positioning: Direct extension of the group's bound-constrained stochastic IPM (Curtis-Kungurtsev-Robinson-Wang 2025); separated from non-Lipschitz stochastic-gradient work because the barrier changes each iteration; claims no comparable stochastic IPM exists; points to stochastic SQP methods for a future infeasible variant (pp. 2-3, 34-35).
writing: Limitations announced upfront ('Let us emphasize upfront' not competitive deterministically); the nonstandard assumption flagged in contributions and given a full section with examples; each parameter rule followed by a design-rationale paragraph and a concrete admissible setting; conclusion explains concretely why a slack-based infeasible variant is hard (pp. 3, 12, 19-20, 25-30, 34-35).
limits_future: Feasible method needing a strictly feasible start; no nonlinear equalities; Assumption 2 parameters not computable in advance (tuning/resets needed); conservative prescribed steps; bounded-error noise; not competitive deterministically. Future: practical directions meeting Assumptions 2/5; a single-loop infeasible IPM (pp. 3, 5, 8, 18, 26-30, 34-35).

method_links.note: One loop without an inner barrier-subproblem test, but the barrier parameter follows a prescribed schedule rather than being steered by measured progress; the code resets mu1 when the direction test fails; feasibility comes from a separate Phase I because a strictly feasible start is required.
Without f_inf, success is judged by a relative stationarity measure whose denominator takes the smaller initial stationarity value, the harder comparison for the method.

No external baseline because none is comparable; the deterministic twin is the reference and all 10 stochastic seeds are printed, but parameters (t = 0.7, mu1 reset factor) are set without a reported tuning procedure.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Section 5 gives a polyhedral example where Assumption 2 holds for large mu/theta and a curved example where the argument breaks, with Fig. 1.

transferable: Shift a log barrier by analysis-only constants so it is bounded below and monotone in mu; the algorithm never needs the constants (pp. 9-10).
Confine a random step-scaling factor to a deterministic band and bound its cross term with the gradient noise by splitting on the sign of the inner product (Lemma 9, pp. 22-23).
Replace a nested barrier loop by prescribed coupled decay of barrier and neighbourhood parameters plus a step cap that keeps the iterate in the current neighbourhood (pp. 6-9).
When no competitor exists, use the deterministic twin as reference, print every seed, and pick convex feasible regions so seed-to-seed differences reflect noise (pp. 32-34).
Give a nonstandard assumption its own section with a holding example, a failing example and a practical fallback (pp. 25-30).
Estimate Lipschitz and bound constants for prescribed step sizes by sampling points around the start (p. 31).

quotes.text: meaning that there is no such method in the literature against which our algorithm can be compared on a level playing field.

This assumption essentially requires that, when an algorithm iterate is close to a constraint boundary, a direction of sufficient descent can be computed that moves sufficiently away from the boundary.
